headline: Bank of England raises Bank Rate to 4% in first increase since August 2023

terms.meaning: The main interest rate set by the Bank of England, which influences what banks charge and pay.
The nine-member group at the Bank that votes on interest rates.
A narrow sea route in the Gulf through which much of the world's oil passes.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises Bank Rate to 4% in first increase since August 2023
levels.body:
The Bank of England raised Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points, from 3.75% to 4%, on Thursday 5 November. It is the first rise in more than three years.
The Monetary Policy Committee voted 8 to 1. The single dissenter wanted a larger rise of 0.5 points, to 4.25%. The Bank expects inflation to climb to about 5% by the middle of 2027, up from 3.5% in the 12 months to September, when motor fuel prices were the main driver.
The Bank blames the rise in energy costs on the war with Iran, which began when the United States and Israel attacked on 28 February, and on bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz. Governor Andrew Bailey said the increase should not be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes, but added that, unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, it does not seem likely to be the last. The next decision is due on 17 December.
levels.why: Higher borrowing costs affect mortgages, loans and savings, and the Bank says inflation could rise much further.

levels.headline: Bank of England lifts interest rate to 4%, the first rise in over three years
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised its main interest rate, Bank Rate, from 3.75% to 4%. It is the first increase since August 2023.
Eight members of the Monetary Policy Committee backed the quarter-point rise. One wanted a bigger move, to 4.25%. The Bank now expects inflation to reach about 5% by mid-2027. In September it stood at 3.5%, pushed up mainly by the price of petrol and diesel.
Officials link the problem to the Iran war and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, which has pushed up energy prices. Governor Andrew Bailey said this should not be seen as the start of a long run of rises, but that more increases look likely unless the conflict in the Middle East ends. The Bank's next rate decision is scheduled for 17 December.
levels.why: The decision changes borrowing costs for households and firms and signals how worried the Bank is about prices.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4% to fight rising inflation
levels.body:
The Bank of England has increased interest rates for the first time in more than three years. Bank Rate rose by a quarter of a percentage point, from 3.75% to 4%.
The committee that sets the rate voted 8 to 1 for the rise. One member wanted a larger increase. The Bank expects inflation, the rate at which prices rise, to reach about 5% by the middle of 2027. It was 3.5% in September, largely because of higher fuel costs.
Policymakers say the war involving Iran is behind much of the pressure, because it has disrupted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. Governor Andrew Bailey said the rise was not the start of a long series of increases, but that further rises seem likely if the conflict continues. The next decision comes on 17 December.
levels.why: Interest rates shape what people pay on mortgages and loans and what they earn on savings.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4%. It is the first rise since August 2023.
Eight of the nine members of the Bank's rate-setting committee voted for the increase. The other wanted a bigger rise, to 4.25%. The Bank expects inflation to hit about 5% by the middle of 2027. In September, prices were rising at 3.5% a year, driven mostly by the cost of fuel for vehicles.
The Bank says higher energy prices caused by the war with Iran, and problems shipping oil through the Strait of Hormuz, are pushing prices up. Governor Andrew Bailey said the rise should not be seen as the first of a long sequence, but did not expect it to be the last unless the Middle East conflict is settled. The next decision is on 17 December.
levels.why: It affects the cost of borrowing for homeowners, businesses and the government.

levels.headline: Bank of England puts up interest rates to 4% as prices keep climbing
levels.body:
The Bank of England has put up its main interest rate, known as Bank Rate, from 3.75% to 4%. This is the first rise in over three years. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive and are meant to slow price rises.
Eight members of the committee voted yes and one wanted an even bigger rise. The Bank thinks inflation, which is how fast prices go up, will reach about 5% by the middle of next year. In September it was 3.5%, mostly because petrol and diesel cost more.
The Bank says the war with Iran is raising energy costs, partly because oil ships are struggling to pass through the Strait of Hormuz. Governor Andrew Bailey said more rises are likely if the conflict goes on, though this is not the start of a long run. The next decision is on 17 December.
levels.why: Rates affect mortgages, loans and savings, so changes can touch most households.

levels.headline: The Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates. The main rate went from 3.75% to 4%. This is the first rise for more than three years. Interest is the extra money you pay when you borrow, or earn when you save.
Banks follow this rate. So higher rates usually mean dearer mortgages and loans, and better pay on savings. The Bank hopes it will slow rising prices. Prices went up by 3.5% in the year to September, mostly because fuel cost more. The Bank thinks the figure may reach about 5% by the middle of 2027.
The Bank says the war with Iran has pushed up energy prices. The head of the Bank, Andrew Bailey, said more rises could follow if the war goes on. The next decision is on 17 December.
levels.why: Rates change what families pay on loans and mortgages and what they earn on savings.

levels.headline: Bank of England puts interest rates up to 4%
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates. It went from 3.75% to 4%. The Bank has not done this for over three years.
An interest rate is the price of borrowing money. When it goes up, loans and mortgages usually cost more. Saving can pay a little more too. The Bank wants to stop prices rising too fast. Prices rose 3.5% in the year to September, mainly because petrol and diesel got dearer. The Bank thinks it could reach about 5% by the middle of next year.
Oil and gas cost more because of the war with Iran. Ships also find it hard to use a key sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. The Bank's boss, Andrew Bailey, said more rises may come if the war goes on. The next decision is on 17 December.
levels.why: Many families will pay more on loans and mortgages, but savers may earn more.

levels.headline: Bank of England makes borrowing a bit dearer
levels.body:
The Bank of England has put up interest rates. They were 3.75% and are now 4%. Interest is the extra money you pay back when you borrow. Mortgages and loans can now cost more.
Prices have been rising fast. This is called inflation. Last year, a pound could buy more than it can now. Petrol and diesel cost more, which pushed prices up by 3.5% in a year. The Bank thinks prices could rise by about 5% by the middle of next year. Raising rates is its way of slowing that down.
There is a war with Iran. It has made oil and gas more expensive. The Bank's boss said more rises could come if the war does not end. The Bank will meet again on 17 December.
levels.why: Your family may pay more on loans, and prices may keep rising for a while.

levels.headline: The Bank of England makes borrowing cost more
levels.body:
There is a bank for the whole country. It is called the Bank of England. It has made it cost more to borrow money. Before, you paid back 3.75 extra for every 100 you borrowed in a year. Now it is 4.
Why? Prices are going up too fast. Things in shops cost more than before. Petrol costs more, too. The Bank wants to slow this down. When borrowing costs more, people spend a bit less. Then prices rise more slowly.
A war far away is part of the problem. It makes oil and gas cost more. The Bank's boss said it may do this again if the war goes on. The Bank will meet again in December.
levels.why: It could make loans and mortgages cost more for grown-ups at home.

levels.headline: A bank makes it cost more to borrow money
levels.body:
Imagine you borrow 10 pounds from a friend for a week. You give back 10 pounds and a little extra as a thank you. That little extra is called interest.
The Bank of England is like the head teacher of all the banks. It sets how much extra people pay when they borrow. This week it said the extra should be a bit bigger. Shop prices have been going up, like sweets costing more pocket money than before. Making borrowing cost more helps prices stop growing so fast.
Prices are going up because oil and gas cost more. That is because of a war far away. The Bank says it may need to do this again if the war carries on.
levels.why: It is a way of stopping prices from rising too fast, so your pocket money can buy more.

headline: S&P 500 jumps 2.35% to 7,549.94 on Monday, its best day since April

terms.meaning: An index tracking 500 large US companies, used to judge how the market is doing.
A fall of more than 10% from a recent high.
A measure of how fast prices for everyday goods and services are rising.

levels.headline: S&P 500 jumps 2.35% to 7,549.94 on Monday, its best day since April
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed up 2.35% at 7,549.94 on Monday 9 November, its best day since 8 April. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 1,104.02 points, or 2.15%, to 52,389.75, and the Nasdaq Composite rose 2.74% to 25,253.14.
The rebound followed a rough week in which the Nasdaq fell into correction territory, meaning it dropped more than 10% from its recent high. Analysts linked the recovery to investors reconsidering fears of slower spending on artificial intelligence and infrastructure, and to lower oil prices.
Tuesday's session had not finished when this edition was written. Investors were waiting for the October US consumer price index, with economists polled by Dow Jones expecting headline prices to rise 0.3% on the month and core prices, which exclude food and energy, 0.2%.
levels.why: Moves of this size in US shares affect pension funds, savings and borrowing costs well beyond Wall Street.

levels.headline: US shares rebound sharply, with the S&P 500 up 2.35% on Monday
levels.body:
US stocks rallied strongly on Monday 9 November. The S&P 500 finished up 2.35% at 7,549.94, its best day since 8 April, while the Dow added 1,104.02 points (2.15%) to close at 52,389.75 and the Nasdaq gained 2.74% to 25,253.14.
The bounce came after a difficult week for technology shares, when the Nasdaq slid into a correction, a fall of more than 10% from its peak. Analysts said investors were rethinking worries that spending on AI and related infrastructure might slow, and were also encouraged by cheaper oil.
The most recent completed session was Monday's. On Tuesday, traders were braced for October's US consumer price index, with forecasts of a 0.3% monthly rise in headline prices and 0.2% in core prices.
levels.why: Share prices feed into pensions and savings, and signal how confident investors are about the economy.

levels.headline: Wall Street has its best day since April as technology shares recover
levels.body:
Wall Street had its strongest day since April on Monday 9 November. The S&P 500 rose 2.35% to 7,549.94. The Dow climbed 1,104.02 points, or 2.15%, to 52,389.75, and the Nasdaq jumped 2.74% to 25,253.14.
It followed a bruising week in which technology shares fell so far that the Nasdaq entered what traders call a correction, a drop of over 10% from its recent high. Analysts said investors were reassessing fears that spending on artificial intelligence might slow, and that falling oil prices also helped.
Attention now turns to US inflation figures for October, due on Tuesday. Economists expect headline prices to rise by 0.3% over the month and core prices, which leave out food and energy, by 0.2%.
levels.why: A recovery in US shares can ease worries about a wider downturn that would affect jobs and investments.

levels.headline: US stocks surge as the S&P 500 posts its best day since April
levels.body:
US stocks surged on Monday 9 November. The S&P 500, a measure of 500 large American companies, rose 2.35% to close at 7,549.94, its best day since April. The Dow gained 2.15% to 52,389.75 and the Nasdaq rose 2.74% to 25,253.14.
The jump followed a week of heavy selling in technology companies, which left the Nasdaq more than 10% below its recent high. Analysts said investors had grown less worried that spending on artificial intelligence would slow, and cheaper oil also lifted the mood.
Investors are now waiting for US consumer price figures for October, which show how fast prices are rising. Forecasts suggest headline prices rose 0.3% in the month and core prices 0.2%.
levels.why: Rising share prices can protect pension pots, but sharp swings show how nervous markets remain.

levels.headline: US shares bounce back strongly, with the S&P 500 up 2.35% in a day
levels.body:
American shares bounced back strongly on Monday 9 November. The S&P 500 index, which tracks 500 big US firms, ended the day up 2.35% at 7,549.94. That was its best day since April. The Dow, another index, rose 2.15% to 52,389.75, and the Nasdaq, which has many tech firms, rose 2.74% to 25,253.14.
The week before had been bad for tech shares. The Nasdaq fell by more than 10% from its high, which is called a correction. Investors had been worried that companies might spend less on artificial intelligence. Those worries eased, and oil got cheaper too.
On Tuesday, people were waiting for new inflation figures, which measure how quickly prices go up. Experts expected prices to rise 0.3% in October.
levels.why: Big moves in the US market can affect savings and pensions around the world.

levels.headline: Stock prices in the US jump by the most since April
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States jumped on Monday 9 November. The main index, the S&P 500, rose by 2.35% to 7,549.94. It was the biggest one-day rise since April. Two other well-known measures also went up: the Dow by 2.15% and the Nasdaq by 2.74%.
The jump came after a bad week. Shares in technology firms had dropped a lot, and the Nasdaq was more than 10% below its top. People had feared that firms would spend less on artificial intelligence. Those fears eased, and cheaper oil also helped.
Next, people are waiting for new inflation figures, which show how fast prices are going up. Experts think prices rose by about 0.3% in October.
levels.why: When shares rise and fall quickly, it can change how safe people feel about their savings.

levels.headline: US share prices go up a lot after a bad week
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States went up a lot on Monday 9 November. A share is a small piece of a company. The S&P 500, a list of 500 big American companies, rose by 2.35%. That is its best day since April.
The week before was bad. Prices of technology companies fell hard. Some investors worried that firms would spend less money on artificial intelligence, or AI. On Monday those worries got smaller. Oil also got cheaper, which helped.
The Dow rose by 2.15% and the Nasdaq rose by 2.74%. On Tuesday, people were waiting for new figures on inflation. Inflation means prices going up over time. Experts thought prices rose by about 0.3% in October.
levels.why: Share prices can change the value of pensions and savings that many families rely on.

levels.headline: American share prices bounce back after a rough week
levels.body:
Share prices in America went up a lot on Monday. A share is a tiny part of a company that people can buy. The S&P 500 is a list of 500 big firms, and its price rose by 2.35%. It was the best day since April.
Last week was hard for technology firms. Their share prices fell a lot, because people worried the firms might spend less on AI, which means smart computer programs. On Monday the worry got smaller, and oil prices also fell. Oil helps run cars and factories, so cheaper oil is good news.
On Tuesday, people waited for new numbers on inflation. That is how fast prices go up in shops.
levels.why: Many people save money in shares, so big changes can matter to families.

levels.headline: Share prices in the US shoot up
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States shot up on Monday. A share is a small piece of a company. People buy shares hoping the company will do well. The main list of 500 big firms went up by 2.35%. That is the best day since April.
The week before, prices fell. Many of the firms that make computer things had lost a lot of value. Some people feared these firms would spend less money on smart computer programs. On Monday, those fears got smaller. Oil got cheaper too, and that helped.
Now people are waiting for news about prices in shops. If prices rise slowly, that is good news for families.
levels.why: Shares are one way people save money, so big changes can matter to families.

levels.headline: Share prices go up, like a toy getting more popular
levels.body:
Share prices in America went up a lot on Monday. Think of a toy that lots of children want. When more children want it, its price goes up. A share is like a tiny piece of a company, and when lots of people want it, its price goes up too.
Last week, grown-ups got worried about some big computer firms, so fewer people wanted their shares and prices dropped. On Monday, the worry got smaller. People wanted the shares again, so the prices went back up. Cheaper oil, which makes cars and factories go, helped too.
It was the best day since April. Now grown-ups are waiting to hear if prices in shops are rising slowly. Slow rises are better for families.
levels.why: Many families keep savings in shares, so these changes can matter to them.

headline: Government unveils 'earned settlement' with 10-year wait for most workers seeking to stay permanently

terms.meaning: Permission to live in the UK permanently, without time limits.
A system where people must meet conditions over time to gain permanent status.
A way of crossing the Channel without permission, often in inflatable boats.

levels.headline: Government unveils 'earned settlement' with 10-year wait for most workers seeking to stay permanently
levels.body:
The government has set out tougher rules for migrants seeking to settle in the UK. The qualifying period for indefinite leave to remain would rise from five years to 10 for most workers, under plans announced by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood. The rules are reportedly due to take effect next year.
The highest earners could settle within three years. People earning more than £50,271, and some public service workers such as doctors, nurses and teachers, could settle after five. Care workers earning £25,000 are exempt and keep the five-year route, after pushback from unions and some Labour figures. Anyone who breached immigration rules must wait at least 20 years, and those who arrived by small boat or other clandestine means face an extra 10 years, up to 30. All applicants must meet four conditions, including a clean criminal record and high-standard English.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the previous government lost control of immigration after Brexit. Settled status will not be removed from anyone who already holds it. The government estimates more than 500,000 people will wait longer than five years. Reform UK has pledged to scrap indefinite leave to remain.
levels.why: The changes affect how long hundreds of thousands of workers must wait for security, and they are a central political issue.

levels.headline: UK sets out tougher settlement rules, doubling the usual wait to 10 years
levels.body:
The government has announced stricter rules for migrants who want to settle permanently in the UK. For most workers, the wait for indefinite leave to remain would double from five years to 10. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood announced the plan, and it is reportedly due to start next year.
Top earners could qualify after three years. Those on more than £50,271, plus some public service workers such as doctors, nurses and teachers, could qualify after five. Care workers on £25,000 are exempt after objections from unions and some Labour MPs. People who broke immigration rules wait at least 20 years, with an extra 10 for small-boat arrivals. Everyone must meet four conditions, including a clean criminal record and good English.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said numbers rose sharply after Brexit under the previous government and that Ms Mahmood has his full support. Existing settled status stays. The government says over 500,000 people will wait longer than five years. Reform UK wants to scrap the system.
levels.why: The rules decide how long migrants who work in the UK must wait for long-term security.

levels.headline: UK to make most migrants wait 10 years to settle permanently
levels.body:
The UK government has announced tougher rules for people who want to settle in Britain for good. Most workers would have to wait 10 years for indefinite leave to remain, instead of five. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood announced the plan, which is reportedly due to start next year.
There are shorter routes. The highest earners could settle after three years. People earning over £50,271, and some public service workers such as doctors, nurses and teachers, would wait five. Care workers on £25,000 keep the five-year route after complaints from unions and some Labour politicians. Those who broke immigration rules face at least 20 years, and those who arrived by small boat face 10 more. All applicants need a clean criminal record and good English.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK lost control of immigration after Brexit. People who already have settled status will keep it. Ministers expect more than 500,000 people to wait longer.
levels.why: It changes the path to permanent life in the UK for workers, and immigration is a key political divide.

levels.headline: Most migrants will wait 10 years to settle in the UK under new rules
levels.body:
The government wants most migrants who work in the UK to wait 10 years before they can settle permanently. Today the wait is usually five years. The Home Secretary, Shabana Mahmood, announced the plan, and it is reportedly meant to start next year.
Some people would wait less. The highest earners could settle after three years. People earning more than £50,271, and some public service workers such as doctors, nurses and teachers, would wait five. Care workers on £25,000 keep the five-year route, after unions and some Labour politicians complained. People who broke the rules would wait at least 20 years, and those who came by small boat would wait 10 years longer. Everyone must have no criminal record and speak good English.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the country lost control of immigration after Brexit. No one who is already settled will lose that status.
levels.why: The rules affect workers, families and employers, and immigration is a major topic in politics.

levels.headline: The UK plans a longer wait for migrants who want to stay for good
levels.body:
The UK government has announced new rules for people from other countries who want to live in Britain permanently. At the moment, most workers can apply after five years. Under the plan, they would have to wait 10 years. It is reportedly due to start next year.
Some people would wait less. Very high earners could apply after three years. People who earn more than £50,271, and some public service workers like doctors, nurses and teachers, would wait five. Care workers who earn £25,000 would also keep the five-year wait. People who broke the rules would wait at least 20 years. People who came by small boat would wait 10 years longer.
Everyone must also have no crime record and speak good English. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said the country lost control of immigration after Brexit. People who are already settled will not lose their status.
levels.why: It decides how long people who work here must wait to feel secure about staying.

levels.headline: Longer wait to stay in the UK for good
levels.body:
The government wants to change the rules for people from other countries who live and work in the UK. Right now, most can ask to stay for ever after five years. The plan is to make them wait 10 years instead. It may start next year.
Some people would wait less. People who earn a lot could ask after three years. Doctors, nurses and teachers could ask after five, and so could care workers. People who broke the rules would wait much longer. Those who came on small boats would wait longer still.
Everyone would also need good English and no crime record. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says the country lost control of immigration after Brexit. People who are already allowed to stay for ever will keep that right.
levels.why: It affects families who want to feel safe and settled in their new home.

levels.headline: New rules make it harder to settle in the UK
levels.body:
The UK has new plans for people from other countries who want to stay for good. Right now, most workers can ask after five years. The government wants them to wait 10 years instead. The plan may start next year.
Some people would wait less. People who earn a lot could ask after three years. Doctors, nurses and teachers could ask after five. So could care workers. People who broke the rules would wait much longer, at least 20 years. People who came across the sea in small boats would wait even longer.
Everyone would also need no crime record and good English. The Prime Minister said the country had lost control of its borders after Brexit. Brexit means the UK left the European Union. People who already have the right to stay will keep it.
levels.why: It affects thousands of families who live and work here and want to stay.

levels.headline: The UK wants people to wait longer before they can stay for good
levels.body:
Some people move to the UK from other countries to work. After a time, they can ask to stay for ever. Now the government wants to make them wait longer. Most would wait 10 years, not five.
Some people would wait less. People who earn a lot of money could ask sooner. So could doctors, nurses and teachers. People who broke the rules would wait much longer. People who came on small boats would wait even longer than that.
Everyone would also need to speak good English and have no crime record. The leader of the government, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, says the country lost control of its borders. People who can already stay for ever will keep that right. Not everyone agrees with the plan.
levels.why: It could change the lives of many families, and people have strong views about it.

levels.headline: Moving to a new country and staying for good
levels.body:
Imagine you move to a new school. You are allowed to stay, but only for a while. After a few years, you can ask to stay for ever. The UK has a rule like this for grown-ups who move here to work.
Until now, they could ask after five years. The government wants them to wait 10 years instead. Some people, like doctors and nurses, would not wait as long. People who broke the rules would have to wait much longer.
Everyone must also learn English well and not have broken the law. Some people think this is fair. Others think it is too hard on people who help the country. Leaders are still talking about it.
levels.why: It changes how long people who work here must wait before they feel they truly belong.

levels.headline: A new rule about staying in the country
levels.body:
Think about joining a club. At first you are a visitor. After some time, you can become a full member. In the UK, grown-ups who come from other countries can become full members too, after a wait.
The wait used to be five years. The leaders now want it to be longer, ten years. It is like the club changing the rule so you must wait twice as long. Some people, like nurses and teachers, would still wait less.
The leaders say they want the rules to be fair and clear. Some people agree. Others say it is too tough on people who work hard. Grown-ups will keep talking about it.
levels.why: It matters to families who want to feel safe and welcome in their new home.

headline: Autumn Budget temporarily doubles bank tax surcharge to 6% as borrowing forecasts rise

terms.meaning: An extra tax charged on top of the normal rate.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, the official forecaster of the public finances.
Limits the government sets itself on borrowing and debt.

levels.headline: Autumn Budget temporarily doubles bank tax surcharge to 6% as borrowing forecasts rise
levels.body:
The Autumn Budget, delivered on 28 October 2026, temporarily raises the Bank Corporation Tax Surcharge from 3% to 6%. The higher rate applies for 15 months, from 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2028, and returns to 3% from 1 April 2028.
The Treasury says the measure raises £1.5 billion to help fund support for households and businesses, while the Office for Budget Responsibility estimates it adds £1 billion to receipts in 2027-28. The OBR's forecast has borrowing at 4.2% of GDP, or £133 billion, this year. Compared with its March forecast, borrowing is higher in every year, by around £18 billion this year, mainly because of higher debt interest costs.
Economic Secretary Lucy Rigby defended the tax, saying it would ease pressure on households amid global volatility. JPMorgan boss Jamie Dimon had lobbied against higher bank taxes, but shares in London-listed lenders rose after the announcement because the increase was smaller than some had feared. The government says the measures are fully funded and meet its fiscal rules.
levels.why: Tax decisions shape support for households and show how much pressure higher borrowing costs put on the public finances.

levels.headline: Budget doubles the bank surcharge for 15 months as borrowing forecast rises
levels.body:
The Budget presented on 28 October raises the tax surcharge on banks from 3% to 6%, but only temporarily. It runs from 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2028 and falls back to 3% on 1 April 2028.
The Treasury expects £1.5 billion to help pay for support for households and businesses. The independent Office for Budget Responsibility puts the gain at £1 billion in 2027-28. It forecasts borrowing of £133 billion, or 4.2% of GDP, this year, about £18 billion more than it predicted in March, mostly because of higher interest on government debt.
Treasury minister Lucy Rigby defended the tax, saying it would help ease pressure on households. Banks had lobbied hard, including JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon, yet shares in London-listed lenders rose because the rise was smaller than feared. Ministers say the plans are fully funded and meet the fiscal rules.
levels.why: It shows how the government is paying for support while borrowing costs rise.

levels.headline: Budget raises tax on banks for 15 months to help fund support for households
levels.body:
The government's Budget on 28 October raises an extra tax on banks. The surcharge goes from 3% to 6% for 15 months, from January 2027 to March 2028. After that it falls back to 3%.
The Treasury says the change raises £1.5 billion to pay for help for households and businesses. The official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility, says the figure is closer to £1 billion in 2027-28. It also expects the government to borrow £133 billion this year, about £18 billion more than it forecast in March, mainly because interest on government debt costs more.
Treasury minister Lucy Rigby said the tax would ease pressure on households. Bank bosses had argued against it, but bank shares rose because the rise was smaller than some feared. The government says its plans are paid for and follow its own borrowing rules.
levels.why: It affects who pays for government support, and how much the state must borrow.

levels.headline: Banks to pay a higher extra tax for 15 months under the Budget
levels.body:
The Budget on 28 October puts up an extra tax on banks. The surcharge goes from 3% to 6%, but only from January 2027 to March 2028. Then it drops back to 3%.
The Treasury says it will bring in £1.5 billion to help pay for support for families and businesses. The Office for Budget Responsibility, the official forecaster, thinks the extra is about £1 billion in 2027-28. It says the government will borrow about £133 billion this year, roughly £18 billion more than it thought in March. The main reason is that interest on the national debt now costs more.
A Treasury minister, Lucy Rigby, said the tax would ease pressure on households. Banks had lobbied against it, but their share prices went up because the rise was smaller than expected. The government says its plans are fully paid for.
levels.why: It shows how the government raises money and how the cost of its debt is growing.

levels.headline: The Budget makes banks pay more tax for a while
levels.body:
The Budget is the government's yearly plan for taxes and spending. This year's, on 28 October, makes banks pay more tax for a short time. The extra tax on banks doubles from 3% to 6%. It lasts from January 2027 until March 2028. After that it goes back to 3%.
The government says this will raise about £1.5 billion to help families and businesses. An independent group that checks the numbers, called the Office for Budget Responsibility, thinks it will raise about £1 billion. It also thinks the government will borrow £133 billion this year. That is £18 billion more than it guessed in March, mostly because interest on old debts costs more.
A minister said the tax would ease pressure on households. Banks did not want it, but their share prices rose because it could have been worse.
levels.why: It helps pay for support at home and shows that the government's debts cost more than before.

levels.headline: Banks will pay a bigger tax for a short time
levels.body:
Every year the government says how it will raise and spend money. This is called the Budget. This year it said banks must pay a bigger extra tax. The extra tax goes from 3 pence in every pound of profit to 6 pence. It will last for 15 months, then fall back.
The government says this will bring in about £1.5 billion. It wants to use it to help families and businesses. A group of experts checks the government's sums. They think the government will borrow £133 billion this year. That is £18 billion more than they thought in March. Interest on old debts has become more expensive.
A minister said the tax would help families with their costs. The banks were not happy, but their share prices went up.
levels.why: The money helps pay for support at home, but the government is also borrowing more.

levels.headline: The government asks banks to pay more tax
levels.body:
The government has a plan for money every year. It is called the Budget. This time, it asked banks to pay more tax for a short while. Banks make big profits. The government will take twice as much of a special extra tax from them.
This will last for 15 months. After that, it goes back to normal. The government says it will raise about £1.5 billion. It plans to use the money to help families and firms. It also has to borrow money, and the interest on its old loans costs more now.
A minister said the extra tax would help families through hard times. Banks had asked the government not to do it.
levels.why: It shows how the country raises money to help families.

levels.headline: Banks are asked to share a little more
levels.body:
A country is a bit like a very big family with one big pot of money. The pot is filled by taxes. Every year the government decides how to fill it and how to spend it. It calls the plan the Budget.
This year the government asked banks to put more into the pot for a short time. Banks earn lots of money, so the government thinks they can share a bit more. The money will help families and businesses who are finding things hard.
The government also borrows money, like taking a loan. Interest on loans costs more than before. Banks did not want to pay more. Even so, the government decided it was fair.
levels.why: It helps the country pay for things that families need.

levels.headline: Sharing out the class tuck shop money
levels.body:
Imagine a class has a tuck shop. Every year the teacher decides how to use the tuck shop money. The teacher also decides who should add a bit more. This is a bit like what the government does with the Budget.
This time, the government asked banks to add more for a while. Banks earn lots of money, like the tuck shop selling lots of crisps. The extra money will help families and businesses who are finding life expensive.
The government also borrows money, and paying back the extra costs more than it used to. Some people think the banks should pay more, and some do not. The government has made its choice.
levels.why: It is a way of paying for help that families may need.

levels.headline: Everyone chips in to a big pot
levels.body:
A country has a very big pot of money. It pays for schools, hospitals and roads. People and companies put money in by paying tax. The government decides how much each should give. This plan is called the Budget.
This year, banks must give more for a short time. Banks earn lots of money from looking after savings and lending. The extra money will help families and businesses with the cost of living.
The country also borrows money, like a big loan. It costs more to pay back than before. Some people say the banks should give more. Others say they should not. The government decided they should, for now.
levels.why: It helps pay for the things everyone uses, like schools and hospitals.

headline: Burnham heads to Brussels for 20 November summit as talk of rejoining the EU grows

terms.meaning: A scheme that puts a price on carbon pollution by making firms buy permits.
A fee on imports made with high carbon pollution.
To become a full member of the European Union again.

levels.headline: Burnham heads to Brussels for 20 November summit as talk of rejoining the EU grows
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will attend a UK-EU summit in Brussels on 20 November, where he will meet European Council President António Costa and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Downing Street says the meeting will review progress since the May 2025 partnership and cover security, illegal migration and cutting red tape for farmers and food businesses.
Items on the table include a food and drink trade deal, a deal on emissions trading, progress towards linking energy systems, a youth experience scheme and deeper cooperation on immigration. A draft reportedly points to linking the UK and EU emissions trading systems, which could exempt goods from both sides' carbon border charges, though the draft could change.
Mr Burnham says the status quo is not good enough and that a serious conversation about long-term options should follow a successful summit. He has not ruled out negotiations on full EU membership. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the UK should first join existing EU defence frameworks and that the sides were not yet at the point of membership talks.
levels.why: The summit could change trade, travel and energy costs, and it frames the debate on how close Britain should be to the EU.

levels.headline: UK and EU prepare for 20 November summit amid debate over closer ties
levels.body:
Andy Burnham will travel to Brussels on 20 November for a UK-EU summit with António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen. The government says it will review progress since the May 2025 partnership, focusing on security, illegal migration and reducing red tape for farmers and food firms.
Possible agreements include a food and drink trade deal, linking the two sides' emissions trading systems, closer energy links, a youth experience scheme and more cooperation on immigration. A draft suggests the carbon-market link could exempt UK and EU goods from each other's carbon border charges, but it may still change.
The Prime Minister says the current relationship is not good enough and that a longer discussion about options should follow. He has not ruled out talks on rejoining the EU. Kaja Kallas, the EU's foreign policy chief, said the UK should first join existing defence frameworks and that membership talks would be difficult.
levels.why: It could cut costs for businesses and shapes the long-term question of Britain's place in Europe.

levels.headline: Prime Minister to meet EU leaders in Brussels on 20 November
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet EU leaders in Brussels on 20 November. He will see António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen. The government says the summit will look at what has been achieved since a May 2025 partnership, and talk about security, illegal migration and less paperwork for farmers and food businesses.
The two sides may agree a trade deal on food and drink, a link between their carbon pricing schemes, a youth experience scheme and more cooperation on migration. A draft says goods from each side could be spared the other's carbon border charges. The draft could change before the summit.
Mr Burnham says staying as things are is not good enough. He wants a serious talk about the long-term relationship after the summit and has not ruled out negotiating a return to the EU. The EU's Kaja Kallas said the UK should first join defence schemes and that talks on membership would be hard.
levels.why: Any deal could affect prices, trade and travel, and fuels the argument about rejoining.

levels.headline: UK and EU leaders to meet in Brussels to try to improve trade and cooperation
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, will go to Brussels on 20 November to meet the leaders of the European Union. The aim is to build on a partnership agreed in May 2025. The talks cover security, illegal migration and cutting red tape for farmers and food firms.
The sides may agree a deal on food and drink trade, link their carbon pricing systems, start a youth experience scheme and work together more on migration. Linking the carbon systems could mean goods are not charged extra carbon fees at each other's borders. This is only in a draft.
Mr Burnham says the way things are now is not good enough. After the summit, he wants a serious talk about options, and he has not ruled out discussing rejoining the EU. The EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said the UK should first join EU defence plans.
levels.why: Deals could make trade easier, and the bigger question is how close the UK should be to the EU.

levels.headline: Britain and the EU will meet to talk about working more closely together
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, will visit Brussels on 20 November. He will meet the top leaders of the European Union. The UK left the EU in 2020, but the two sides have been working on a new partnership since May 2025.
They will talk about safety, people crossing the sea illegally, and less paperwork for farmers and food firms. They may agree on trade in food and drink. They may also link their schemes that put a price on pollution. That could stop extra pollution charges on goods crossing the border. A youth scheme could let young people live and work abroad.
Mr Burnham says things as they are now are not good enough. He wants a big talk about the future afterwards. He has not ruled out rejoining the EU. An EU leader said the UK should first join EU defence plans.
levels.why: It could make trade easier and keep alive the question of whether Britain should rejoin.

levels.headline: Britain and Europe meet to talk about being better friends
levels.body:
The UK used to be in a group of countries called the European Union, or EU. It left in 2020. This is called Brexit. Now the leaders want to work together more. On 20 November, the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, will go to Brussels to meet the EU's bosses.
They will talk about keeping people safe, about people crossing the sea in boats, and about trade. They might agree to make it easier to sell food and drink. They might also agree a plan for charging firms for pollution that works in both places.
Mr Burnham says the way things are now is not good enough. He has not said no to the idea of rejoining. An EU leader said it is too early.
levels.why: It could make buying and selling things easier, and it keeps alive a big question about Brexit.

levels.headline: The UK and Europe want to work together more
levels.body:
The UK used to belong to a club of European countries called the EU. In 2020 it left. That is called Brexit. Now the UK leader, Andy Burnham, wants to work more closely with the EU again.
On 20 November he will go to Brussels, where the EU has its main offices, to talk to its leaders. They will talk about trade, safety, and young people living in each other's countries. Trade means buying and selling things across borders. They might make food and drink easier to sell. They might also share rules about pollution.
Mr Burnham says things now are not good enough. He has not said no to rejoining the EU one day. Some EU leaders say it is too soon.
levels.why: It might change what things cost and how easy it is to travel and trade.

levels.headline: The UK and Europe meet to talk about being friends again
levels.body:
The UK used to be in a group with many other European countries. The group is called the EU. The UK left it in 2020, and that is called Brexit. Now the UK leader wants to be closer to the EU again.
He is called the Prime Minister. His name is Andy Burnham. He is going to a city called Brussels on 20 November to meet the EU leaders. They will talk about being safe and about selling things to each other. They might make it easier to sell food and drink.
Some people want the UK to join the EU again. Others do not. The Prime Minister has not said no. An EU leader said it is too early to talk about that.
levels.why: It might change what things cost and how easy it is to trade with our neighbours.

levels.headline: Two neighbours meet to talk about getting closer
levels.body:
Imagine two schools that used to share one playground. One day one school decided to build its own playground. Now they live next door but do not share any more. The UK and the EU are a bit like those schools.
The UK left the EU in 2020. The leader of the UK, Andy Burnham, is going to meet the EU's leaders on 20 November. They will talk about sharing things like keeping people safe, and selling food and drink to each other.
Some people want the UK to go back to the EU. Others do not. Mr Burnham has not said no. An EU leader said it is too soon to talk about that.
levels.why: It could change what things cost and how easily we can work with our neighbours.

levels.headline: Next-door neighbours meet to talk about sharing
levels.body:
Imagine two neighbours who used to share a garden. One day they stopped sharing. Now they want to talk about whether they could share again.
The UK is one neighbour. The EU, which is a group of many countries, is the other. The UK left the group a few years ago. The UK's leader, Andy Burnham, is going to meet the other leaders on 20 November.
They will talk about being safe, and about swapping things, such as food and drink. Some grown-ups would like the UK to join the group again. Others do not. Nobody has decided yet.
levels.why: It is about how neighbours can work together and share.

headline: Rubio says Iran talks are far from a breakthrough as oil slips on Trump's restraint

terms.meaning: The international benchmark price for oil.
Penalties that limit a country's trade and finances.
A narrow Gulf waterway through which much of the world's oil passes.

levels.headline: Rubio says Iran talks are far from a breakthrough as oil slips on Trump's restraint
levels.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday 9 November that talks with Iran are not close to a breakthrough, calling some Iranian demands unacceptable and in some cases outrageous. Iran's Foreign Ministry says Tehran wants US sanctions lifted and the war ended on all fronts before negotiations begin.
President Donald Trump meanwhile said renewed attacks on Iran were unlikely provided talks keep moving, and Brent crude fell on Monday. It had already dropped 16% the previous week to a two-month low of $93.22 a barrel. Analysts at Eurasia Group put the chance of renewed US strikes at 60%, down from 65%.
Shipping has still been hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf waterway through which much of the world's oil passes. Eurasia Group said escalation could send Brent to between $110 and $125.
levels.why: Oil prices feed into petrol, heating and inflation, so the Iran talks matter to household bills.

levels.headline: Iran talks stall publicly while oil prices ease on Trump's softer tone
levels.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday 9 November that talks with Iran are not near a breakthrough and described some Iranian demands as outrageous. Iran says it wants US sanctions lifted and the war ended on every front before it will negotiate.
President Trump said new attacks were unlikely if talks make progress, and oil prices dipped. Brent crude had already fallen 16% the previous week to a two-month low of $93.22 a barrel. Eurasia Group now rates the chance of renewed US strikes at 60%, down from 65%.
Fighting has not stopped completely: both sides report ships hit near the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow route for much of the world's oil. Eurasia Group warned an escalation could lift Brent to between $110 and $125.
levels.why: The outcome affects energy prices and therefore inflation and interest rates around the world.

levels.headline: Oil eases as Trump downplays new strikes, though Rubio sees no Iran breakthrough
levels.body:
Oil prices eased on Monday 9 November after President Trump said fresh attacks on Iran were unlikely as long as talks continue. Yet Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the talks were not close to a breakthrough and called some Iranian demands outrageous.
Iran says it wants US sanctions lifted and the war ended on all fronts before negotiations start. Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, fell 16% the week before to a two-month low of $93.22 a barrel. Analysts at Eurasia Group put the chance of renewed US strikes at 60%, down from 65%.
Ships have still been hit near the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow channel carrying much of the world's oil. Eurasia Group said an escalation could push Brent up to a range of $110 to $125.
levels.why: Higher oil prices push up petrol and energy bills, which can keep inflation and interest rates high.

levels.headline: Oil prices dip as Trump signals restraint, but Iran talks look far from a deal
levels.body:
Oil prices dipped on Monday 9 November after President Trump said new strikes on Iran were unlikely if talks keep moving. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio said a breakthrough was not close and called some of Iran's demands outrageous.
Iran wants US sanctions lifted and the war ended on all fronts before it talks. Brent crude, the main global oil price, fell 16% last week to a two-month low of $93.22 a barrel. Analysts at Eurasia Group put the chance of new US strikes at 60%, down from 65%.
Both sides say ships have been hit near the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea route through which much of the world's oil travels. Eurasia Group said a wider conflict could push Brent to between $110 and $125.
levels.why: Oil prices affect what people pay for petrol and heating, and how fast prices rise generally.

levels.headline: Oil gets cheaper as Trump goes easy on Iran, but a peace deal still looks far away
levels.body:
Oil got cheaper on Monday 9 November. President Trump said new attacks on Iran were unlikely as long as talks go on. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the talks were not close to a deal, and he called some of Iran's demands outrageous.
Iran says it wants US sanctions, which are penalties on its trade, lifted first. It also wants the war ended on all fronts. Brent crude, a key oil price, dropped 16% last week to $93.22 a barrel. A research group, Eurasia Group, thinks there is a 60% chance of new US strikes.
Ships have still been hit near the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route for much of the world's oil. Eurasia Group says that if fighting grows, oil could cost $110 to $125.
levels.why: When oil costs more, petrol, heating and many goods cost more as well.

levels.headline: Oil prices fall a little, but talks with Iran are stuck
levels.body:
Oil prices fell a little on Monday 9 November. US President Donald Trump said new attacks on Iran were unlikely if talks keep going. But the US foreign minister, Marco Rubio, said a deal was not close. He called some of what Iran wants outrageous.
Iran wants the US to drop its sanctions, which are limits on trade, and to end the war everywhere before it will talk. Brent crude, an oil price used around the world, fell by 16% last week to $93.22 a barrel. One research group puts the chance of new US strikes at 60%.
Ships are still being hit near the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea road that carries much of the world's oil. If fighting grows, oil could cost $110 to $125 a barrel.
levels.why: Oil prices change what we pay for petrol and heating, so what happens with Iran can reach our homes.

levels.headline: Oil gets cheaper while the US and Iran argue
levels.body:
Oil got cheaper on Monday 9 November. US President Donald Trump said he did not expect new attacks on Iran if talks go on. But the US foreign minister, Marco Rubio, said the two sides were not close to a deal. He called some of Iran's demands outrageous.
Iran wants the US to drop its sanctions, which are limits on trade, and end the war everywhere before it will talk. Brent, a kind of oil used as a world price, fell 16% last week to $93.22 a barrel. A barrel is a large container for oil. One research group says new US strikes have a 60% chance.
Ships have still been hit near the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea road for much of the world's oil. If the fighting grows, oil could cost much more, and so could petrol.
levels.why: Oil prices change what families pay for petrol and heating.

levels.headline: The price of oil dips while the US and Iran still disagree
levels.body:
The price of oil dipped on Monday 9 November. The US president, Donald Trump, said he did not expect new attacks on Iran if talks continue. But the US foreign minister, Marco Rubio, said no deal was close. He said some of Iran's demands were outrageous.
Iran says the US must end its sanctions, which are rules that stop it trading, and stop the war everywhere first. Oil is sold by the barrel, a big container. A type called Brent fell by 16% last week to $93.22 a barrel.
Ships have still been hit near the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow stretch of sea that much of the world's oil sails through. If the fighting grows, a barrel could cost far more. That would make petrol dearer.
levels.why: Oil makes petrol and heating, so its price can change how much families pay.

levels.headline: Oil gets a bit cheaper, but two countries still disagree
levels.body:
Oil got a bit cheaper on Monday. Oil is a thick liquid from under the ground. It is used to make petrol for cars and to heat buildings. The leader of the United States, Donald Trump, said he did not plan new attacks on Iran while talks go on.
But another US leader, Marco Rubio, said the two countries were not close to agreeing. Iran wants the US to stop blocking its trade and to end the war. The US says some of these wants are not fair.
Ships have still been hit near the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea path for oil ships. If the fighting grows, oil could cost much more, and so could petrol. That is why people watch this closely.
levels.why: Oil prices change what families pay for petrol and heating.

levels.headline: Oil gets a little cheaper, like sweets in the tuck shop
levels.body:
Oil got a little cheaper on Monday. Oil is what makes cars go and keeps many buildings warm. When oil costs more, lots of things in shops cost more, like sweets at the tuck shop when the sugar gets dearer.
Two countries, the United States and Iran, are in a big fight. They are talking to try to stop it. One leader said he did not plan new attacks while they talk. That made oil cheaper. But another leader said they were not close to making peace yet.
Ships carrying oil have still been hit on a narrow sea path. If the fight grows, oil could cost much more again. Grown-ups are watching closely.
levels.why: When oil costs more, many things cost more, and that matters to families.

headline: Supreme Court hears Palestine Action's appeal against its terror ban; ruling awaited

terms.meaning: Officially banning a group as a terrorist organisation under UK law.
The highest court in the UK for most cases.

levels.headline: Supreme Court hears Palestine Action's appeal against its terror ban; ruling awaited
levels.body:
The UK Supreme Court heard a two-day appeal on 4 and 5 November against the government's proscription of Palestine Action as a terrorist group. Huda Ammori, who co-founded the group, was granted permission to challenge the ban on a narrow procedural ground: that the Home Office did not follow its own criteria. No judgment has been reported yet.
The High Court ruled in February that the ban was disproportionate, but the Court of Appeal overturned that decision in June. Ammori has said she would take the case to the European Court of Human Rights if she loses.
Police arrested supporters outside the Supreme Court on 4 November. More than 4,000 arrests have been made under the ban, which makes it a criminal offence to show support for the group.
levels.why: The ruling will decide whether a major use of UK terrorism powers against a protest group stands.

levels.headline: Palestine Action ban: Supreme Court hears appeal, judgment still to come

The Supreme Court heard an appeal on 4 and 5 November against the proscription of Palestine Action under terrorism law. Huda Ammori, a co-founder, was allowed to argue on a narrow ground: that the Home Office failed to follow its own criteria. No ruling has been reported.

levels.why: The case tests how far terrorism powers can be used against protest groups.

The UK's highest court, the Supreme Court, has heard a case about the ban on Palestine Action. The government banned the group by calling it a terrorist group. The court met for two days, on 4 and 5 November. We do not yet know what it will decide.

levels.headline: The top UK court has looked at the ban on Palestine Action

The top court in the UK, the Supreme Court, has looked at the ban on a group called Palestine Action. The government banned it by calling it a terrorist group. Judges listened for two days, on 4 and 5 November. They have not said yet what they decide.

levels.headline: Judges hear a case about a banned protest group

The most senior judges in the UK have heard a case about a group called Palestine Action. The government banned the group and said it was a terrorist group. That means it is against the law to say you support it. The judges listened on 4 and 5 November. They will tell us their decision later.

levels.headline: Judges hear a case about a group that the government banned

levels.why: Courts check that governments follow their own rules, and this case tests that.

levels.headline: Judges hear a case about a group that was banned

levels.headline: Judges listen to a big argument about a banned group
levels.body:
Some very important judges have been listening to an argument. It is about a group of people who protest. The government banned the group and said it was dangerous. Now, saying you like the group is against the law. The judges listened for two days. We are still waiting for them to decide.
One woman who helped start the group says the government did not follow its own rules. Judges are like referees in a game. They check that everybody follows the rules, even the government.
Lots of people have been arrested for saying they support the group. Now everyone is waiting to hear if the judges think the ban was fair.
levels.why: Judges make sure everyone follows the rules, even the government.

headline: US-hosted Ukraine-Russia peace talks begin in Abu Dhabi as Europe seeks a seat

terms.meaning: Negotiations involving three parties, here Ukraine, Russia and the United States.

levels.headline: US-hosted Ukraine-Russia peace talks begin in Abu Dhabi as Europe seeks a seat
levels.body:
Peace talks between Ukraine and Russia, hosted by the United States, are due in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November, the first trilateral negotiations since February. Russia's delegation is led by Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky, and the US side includes envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
The EU is sending a joint team, alongside France, Germany and the UK, though it is unclear whether Europeans will meet the Russians face to face. President Trump has spoken of a strong inclination to end the war and has said post-war Ukraine will have a different shape.
The core dispute is territorial. Vladimir Putin has demanded that Ukraine withdraw from four regions Moscow claimed to annex in 2022, while Ukraine rejects ceding territory. On 7 November Russia struck power facilities around Kyiv and damaged a major bridge.
levels.why: The talks could shape European security, energy prices and defence spending for years.

levels.headline: Ukraine and Russia due to hold US-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi as strikes continue

Ukraine and Russia are due to hold US-hosted talks in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November, their first three-way negotiations with the United States since February. Russia's delegation is led by Vladimir Medinsky, and Washington is sending envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

levels.headline: Peace talks on Ukraine open in Abu Dhabi with the main dispute unresolved

Ukraine and Russia are sending delegations to Abu Dhabi for talks on 10 and 11 November, hosted by the United States. It is the first time the three have met since February. Russia's team is led by Vladimir Medinsky, and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will take part.
The EU is sending a joint team, together with France, Germany and the UK, although it is not certain they will meet the Russians directly. President Trump says he sees a strong inclination to end the war.
The main sticking point is land. Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to withdraw from four regions Russia says it annexed in 2022, an annexation most countries do not recognise. Ukraine refuses. Russia struck power facilities near Kyiv on 7 November.
levels.why: A deal or a failure would affect European security and energy costs.

levels.headline: Ukraine and Russia meet for peace talks in Abu Dhabi, but they disagree about land

levels.why: The talks could decide whether the war ends and how safe Europe feels.

levels.headline: Ukraine and Russia hold peace talks in Abu Dhabi

Ukraine and Russia are holding peace talks in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November. The United States is the host. It is the first meeting of the three countries since February. Russia's team is led by Vladimir Medinsky. Two US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, are there too.

levels.why: If the talks work, the war could end. If not, the fighting may go on.

levels.headline: Ukraine and Russia talk about peace in Abu Dhabi

Ukraine and Russia are talking about peace in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November. The United States is the host. It is the first time the three have met since February. Russia's team is led by Vladimir Medinsky, and the US has sent two envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
