levels.headline: Ukraine and Russia talk about peace in the United Arab Emirates
levels.body:
Ukraine and Russia are talking about peace this week in Abu Dhabi, a city in the United Arab Emirates. The talks are on 10 and 11 November. The United States invited both sides. They have not all met like this since February.
The war began when Russia attacked Ukraine. Other countries in Europe want to help. The European Union is sending a team, as are France, Germany and the UK. It is not clear if they will meet the Russians face to face.
The hardest thing to agree on is land. Russia's leader, Vladimir Putin, wants Ukraine to give up four regions. Ukraine says no. Just days ago, Russia hit power sites near the capital, Kyiv.
levels.why: Peace would end the suffering in Ukraine and make Europe feel safer.

levels.headline: Two countries at war meet to try to talk about peace
levels.body:
Two countries at war, Russia and Ukraine, are meeting this week to talk about peace. They are meeting in Abu Dhabi, a city far away from both of them. The talks are on 10 and 11 November. The United States is helping to run them.
Other countries in Europe want to help too. They are sending a team, but nobody is sure if they will sit with the Russians. The US president says he wants the war to end.
The hardest part is land. Russia wants Ukraine to give up four regions. Ukraine says they belong to Ukraine, and it will not give them up. Just days ago, Russia hit power stations near the city of Kyiv, so people there lost light and heat.
levels.why: Peace would help the people of Ukraine and make Europe safer.

levels.headline: Two sides in a big argument sit down to talk, like at school
levels.body:
Imagine two children who have been fighting for a very long time. A teacher invites them to sit down and talk. That is what is happening this week. Russia and Ukraine are two countries that have been at war, and they are meeting in a city called Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November.
The United States is like the teacher helping them. Other countries in Europe want to help too, and they are sending a team to listen.
The hard part is that they disagree about who owns some land. Russia wants Ukraine to give up four regions. Ukraine says no. Just days ago, Russia hit power stations near Kyiv, so some families lost light and heat. Everyone hopes the talk helps the fighting stop.
levels.why: If the talks work, children and families in Ukraine could be safe again.

headline: Democrats win control of both chambers of Congress in midterm rejection of Trump

terms.meaning: US elections held halfway through a president's four-year term.
A Senate rule that usually needs 60 votes to pass most laws.
A president's power to block a law passed by Congress.

levels.headline: Democrats win control of both chambers of Congress in midterm rejection of Trump
levels.body:
Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in the US midterm elections on 3 November, giving them a majority in each chamber for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term. Counts were still continuing, so seat totals vary by source.
CNBC's election desk projected Democrats at at least 250 House seats, and on track for at least 54 Senate seats, with gains in states including Texas, Ohio, Kansas and Maine. A Mississippi Senate race was still very close. Euronews said the result reflected anger over living costs, tariffs and the war against Iran.
Mr Trump told the New York Times he was absolutely willing to accept the results and told Fox News he plans to use his veto. Democrats lack the two-thirds majorities needed to override a veto and will fall short of the 60 Senate votes needed to beat the filibuster on most laws. They are expected to launch investigations into the Iran war, immigration enforcement and corruption allegations, and to block appointments.
levels.why: Control of Congress limits what the president can pass, and it can change US policy on trade, war and spending.

levels.headline: Democrats take both houses of Congress in a sweeping midterm result
levels.body:
Democrats won both the House of Representatives and the Senate on 3 November, handing them a majority in each chamber for Donald Trump's last two years. Some counts are unfinished.
CNBC projected at least 250 House seats and at least 54 Senate seats for Democrats, who flipped seats in Texas, Ohio, Kansas, Maine and elsewhere. The Mississippi Senate race was too close to call. Euronews reported anger over living costs, tariffs and the war with Iran as drivers of the result.
Mr Trump said he would accept the results and also said he plans to use his veto power. Democrats cannot override a veto without Republican help, and they remain short of 60 Senate votes to bypass the filibuster. They are expected to investigate the Iran war, immigration enforcement and corruption allegations, and to block Mr Trump's agenda and senior appointments.
levels.why: It will change what the White House can achieve and may affect markets, trade and foreign policy.

levels.headline: Democrats win control of the US Congress
levels.body:
The Democratic Party has won control of both parts of the US Congress, the House of Representatives and the Senate, in elections held on 3 November. These are called the midterms because they take place halfway through a president's term. Counting is not finished.
CNBC says Democrats will have at least 250 House seats and at least 54 Senate seats. They won seats in states including Texas and Ohio. One Senate race in Mississippi is very close. Euronews says voters were angry about living costs, tariffs and the war with Iran.
President Trump says he accepts the result but plans to use his veto, which lets him block laws. Democrats do not have enough votes to overrule him. They also cannot beat the Senate rule that needs 60 votes for most laws. They are expected to investigate the Iran war and immigration enforcement.
levels.why: It limits the president's power and could change US policy.

levels.headline: Democrats take control of both houses of the US Congress
levels.body:
Voters in the United States have given the Democratic Party control of both houses of Congress, the House of Representatives and the Senate. The vote was on 3 November, halfway through President Donald Trump's four-year term. Counting is still going on.
Democrats are projected to hold at least 250 of the 435 House seats and at least 54 Senate seats. They won seats in places like Texas, Ohio and Maine. News reports say many voters were unhappy about prices, tariffs and the war with Iran.
Mr Trump says he accepts the result but will use his veto to block laws he dislikes. Democrats do not have enough votes to overrule a veto. They are expected to hold investigations into the Iran war and immigration enforcement.
levels.why: It means the president cannot easily pass new laws, and it may shift US policy.

levels.headline: Democrats win big in US elections and take over Congress
levels.body:
Voters in the United States held elections on 3 November. The Democratic Party won control of both parts of Congress, which is where US laws are made. The two parts are called the House and the Senate. Counting is not quite finished.
The elections were halfway through the term of President Donald Trump, who is a Republican. Many voters were unhappy about high prices, taxes on imports called tariffs, and the war with Iran. Democrats won seats in several states, including Texas and Ohio.
The president says he accepts the result. But he also says he will use his veto, which means he can say no to a law. Democrats do not have enough votes to overrule him. They plan to ask hard questions about the war and other things.
levels.why: It means the president has less power to do what he wants.

levels.headline: Democrats win control of the US parliament
levels.body:
In the United States, the group that makes the laws is called Congress. Voters chose who should be in it on 3 November. The Democratic Party won most seats in both parts of Congress. Counting is still going on.
President Donald Trump is from the Republican Party. He is the head of the government. But he cannot make laws on his own. Congress must agree. Now the other party is in charge of Congress. Many voters said they were unhappy about prices and the war with Iran.
The president says he accepts the result. But he says he will say no to laws he does not like. Democrats do not have enough votes to overrule him. They will also ask questions about the war.
levels.why: The president will find it harder to get his plans passed.

levels.headline: US voters choose a new team in charge of lawmaking
levels.body:
In America, the people who make the laws are called Congress. Voters pick them. On 3 November there was a vote. The Democratic Party, one of the two main teams, won most seats. They now control the whole of Congress.
The President, Donald Trump, belongs to the other team, the Republicans. He is in charge of the country. But he needs Congress to agree to new laws. Now the other team has the most votes in Congress. Many voters said they were unhappy about prices and about a war with Iran.
The President says he accepts the result. But he can still say no to a law. This is called a veto. The other team does not have enough votes to overrule it.
levels.why: The President will find it harder to get his ideas turned into laws.

levels.headline: The other team wins the vote in America
levels.body:
America has a president. He is called Donald Trump. He is the leader of the country. But he cannot make laws on his own. A group called Congress has to agree. People vote to choose who sits in Congress.
This week people voted. The other team, called the Democrats, won most seats. The president's team, called the Republicans, lost. Many voters said things cost too much. Some were unhappy about a war.
The president says he accepts the result. He can still say no to new laws. The Democrats will ask the president hard questions. Everyone will watch what happens next.
levels.why: It changes who has the power to make rules in America.

levels.headline: A class vote has a surprise winner
levels.body:
Imagine a class has a leader. The leader is the class captain. The captain can suggest ideas. But the class must vote on them. This is like how America works, with a president and a group of lawmakers.
This week, the class voted for the group of lawmakers. The team that does not agree with the captain won. Many children said they were unhappy that things cost too much.
The captain says he accepts the vote. But he can still say no to some ideas. The new team will ask the captain questions. It will be harder for the captain to get all his ideas passed.
levels.why: It means the leader has to listen more.

levels.headline: Voting for who makes the rules
levels.body:
Imagine a school where the pupils vote for a council. The council decides some rules. The headteacher also has a say, but the council has power too. America works a bit like that.
This week American grown-ups voted. The team that did not agree with the president won most seats. That means the president will find it harder to get his own way.
Many voters said they were unhappy about things costing too much. The winning team says it will ask the president lots of questions. The president says he will say no to rules he does not like.
levels.why: It decides who has power to make the rules.

headline: US economy adds 165,000 jobs in October, far above forecasts, as unemployment slips to 4.1%

terms.meaning: The number of paid jobs in the economy.
The share of people looking for work who cannot find it.
The US central bank, which sets interest rates.

levels.headline: US economy adds 165,000 jobs in October, far above forecasts, as unemployment slips to 4.1%
levels.body:
The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October, well above the consensus forecast of about 59,000, according to figures released on 6 November. The unemployment rate edged down to 4.1% from a forecast of 4.2%. Gains came in professional and business services, healthcare and manufacturing, and figures for August and September were revised up.
Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% on the month and 3.1% over the year. There were weaker signs under the surface: a broader measure of unemployment, which includes discouraged workers and people in part-time jobs who want full-time work, rose 0.3 percentage points to 7.9%. The average length of unemployment jumped to 27.1 weeks, the highest since September 2021.
The 10-year Treasury yield rose after the report. Investors judged that it strengthens the case for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again at its meeting next month, with inflation still above its 2% target.
levels.why: Strong jobs data can push up interest rates, which affects borrowing costs well beyond the US.

levels.headline: October jobs report beats forecasts and raises odds of another Fed rate rise
levels.body:
US employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far more than the roughly 59,000 economists expected. The unemployment rate fell slightly to 4.1%. The report came out on 6 November. Professional services, healthcare and manufacturing led the gains, and earlier months were revised higher.
Pay rose 0.4% in the month and 3.1% over the year. But a broader unemployment measure rose to 7.9%, and the typical time spent jobless reached 27.1 weeks, the longest since September 2021, so the picture is not all positive.
Government bond yields rose and investors now see a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to lift interest rates in December, because inflation remains above the bank's 2% target.
levels.why: A strong labour market makes the Fed less likely to cut rates and more likely to raise them.

levels.headline: US employers add far more jobs than expected in October
levels.body:
American employers created 165,000 new jobs in October. Experts had expected only about 59,000. The unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%. The figures came out on 6 November. Most new jobs were in business services, healthcare and factories. The numbers for August and September were also raised.
Wages grew 0.4% in the month and 3.1% over the year. Still, there were worrying signs. A wider measure of unemployment rose to 7.9%. People who are out of work are taking longer to find jobs, on average 27.1 weeks, the longest since September 2021.
After the report, investors thought the Federal Reserve might raise interest rates again at its next meeting, in December. Prices are still rising faster than the bank's 2% goal.
levels.why: Interest rates in the US influence borrowing costs and share prices worldwide.

levels.headline: US adds many more jobs than expected in October
levels.body:
The US economy created 165,000 jobs in October. Experts had guessed about 59,000. The share of people looking for work who could not find it fell a little, to 4.1%. The numbers were published on 6 November. New jobs were mostly in business services, healthcare and factories.
Pay went up 0.4% in the month and 3.1% over the year. But some signs were less good. A wider measure of people without enough work rose to 7.9%. People out of work now take 27.1 weeks on average to find a job, the longest since September 2021.
Investors now think the Federal Reserve, the US central bank, may raise interest rates again in December. Prices are still rising faster than the bank wants, which is 2% a year.
levels.why: A strong jobs market can lead to higher interest rates.

levels.headline: More Americans found jobs than experts expected
levels.body:
The US had a strong month for jobs in October. Employers added 165,000 new jobs. Experts had thought it would be only about 59,000. The share of people without a job fell to 4.1%. This was announced on 6 November.
Most new jobs were in healthcare, business services and factories. Pay went up a little too. But it was not all good news. More people are working part-time when they want full-time work. People who lose their jobs are taking longer to find new ones, more than 27 weeks on average.
Because the jobs news was strong, some investors think the Federal Reserve, which sets US interest rates, may raise them again in December. Prices are still rising too fast for the bank.
levels.why: Strong jobs can lead to higher interest rates, which affect loans.

levels.headline: A strong month for jobs in America
levels.body:
America had a good month for jobs in October. Employers hired 165,000 more people. Experts had only expected about 59,000. Out of every 100 people who wanted to work, about four could not find a job. That is a low number.
Many of the new jobs were in hospitals, offices and factories. Wages also went up. But some people are finding it hard. Those who lose a job now wait a long time to find a new one, over six months on average.
The news may lead the bank that sets American interest rates to raise them again in December. When interest rates go up, borrowing gets more expensive. Prices are still going up faster than the bank wants.
levels.why: It can change what borrowing costs in the US and beyond.

levels.headline: More people in America got jobs last month
levels.body:
Last month in America, many more people got jobs than experts thought. Employers hired 165,000 people. The experts had guessed about 59,000. About four in every 100 people who wanted a job could not find one.
New jobs came in hospitals, offices and factories. Wages went up a little. But finding a job is slow for some people. If you lose your job, it can take more than six months to find a new one.
Because the news was good, the bank that sets America's interest rates may raise them again in December. This is the Federal Reserve. Higher rates make loans cost more. Prices are still going up too fast.
levels.why: It may change how much loans cost.

levels.headline: America found lots of new jobs last month
levels.body:
Many people in America got new jobs last month. Employers hired 165,000 more workers. Experts had thought it would be much fewer. About four in every 100 people who wanted work could not find it.
The new jobs were in hospitals, offices and factories. Workers also got paid a little more. Some people still find it hard to get a new job after losing one. It can take over six months.
A big bank in America looks at jobs to decide on interest rates. Because there were lots of jobs, it may raise rates in December. That makes loans cost more.
levels.why: It may make loans cost more.

levels.headline: Lots of new jobs for grown-ups
levels.body:
Grown-ups go to work to earn money. In America last month, many more grown-ups found work than people expected. It was 165,000 more jobs. They work in places like hospitals, offices and factories.
Some people still find it hard to get a job. When they lose one, it can take over six months to find another. That is a long time.
A bank in America looks at jobs when it decides about interest rates. Interest is the extra you pay back on a loan. With so many jobs, the bank may make it bigger in December.
levels.why: It tells us how well grown-ups are doing at finding work.

levels.headline: More grown-ups have jobs
levels.body:
Many grown-ups go to work to earn money. They might work in a hospital, a shop or a factory. In America last month, lots more grown-ups found jobs than anyone guessed.
It is like when a class expects five new pupils to join and fifty join instead. That is a nice surprise. But some grown-ups still find it hard to find work after losing a job. It can take months.
A bank in America watches how many people have jobs. If lots of people have jobs, it may make borrowing cost more. This is to stop prices rising too fast.
levels.why: It shows how many families have money coming in.

headline: Israel's president tasks Netanyahu rival Eisenkot with forming a government

terms.meaning: Israel's parliament, which has 120 seats.
A group of parties that join together to form a government.
The formal authority to try to form a government.

levels.headline: Israel's president tasks Netanyahu rival Eisenkot with forming a government
levels.body:
Israel's president, Isaac Herzog, has asked opposition figure Gadi Eisenkot to try to form the next government, a setback for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. After consultations, factions with 67 members of the Knesset backed Mr Eisenkot, against 46 for Mr Netanyahu, the president's office said.
Neither bloc has a majority after last month's election. Mr Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats and Mr Eisenkot's 48, short of the 61 needed in the 120-seat Knesset. Likud remained the largest party, and Arab parties won a record 19 seats between them, making them potential kingmakers. Mr Eisenkot's allies largely resist relying on them, and he could try for a minority government with outside support, which others in his bloc have said they would reject.
Mr Eisenkot has 28 days to form a government, extendable by 14. If he fails, the president can offer the mandate to someone else, and a new election could follow. Mr Netanyahu called for a national unity government and alleged Arab parties stole the vote, but the election commission found no fraud.
levels.why: The outcome will shape Israel's approach to the war in Gaza and the wider region.

levels.headline: Eisenkot given first chance to form Israel's next government
levels.body:
President Isaac Herzog has given opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot the first chance to build a coalition, after factions representing 67 MPs backed him against 46 for Benjamin Netanyahu.
Nobody has a majority. Mr Netanyahu's bloc won 53 of the 120 Knesset seats and Mr Eisenkot's won 48, with 61 needed. Likud is still the biggest party, and Arab parties won a record 19 seats between them. Mr Eisenkot's allies mostly do not want to depend on them, and some reject a minority government supported from outside.
He has 28 days, which can be extended by 14. If he cannot succeed, the mandate may go to someone else, or Israel may go back to the polls. Mr Netanyahu wants a national unity government and says Arab parties stole the election, though the election commission found no evidence of fraud.
levels.why: A new government would set Israel's direction on Gaza, the Iran war and relations with the US.

levels.headline: Israel's president picks Netanyahu's rival to try to form a government
levels.body:
Israel's president, Isaac Herzog, has asked Gadi Eisenkot to try to form the next government. This is a setback for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Parties with 67 members of parliament backed Mr Eisenkot, and parties with 46 backed Mr Netanyahu.
The election did not give anyone a majority. Mr Netanyahu's group won 53 seats and Mr Eisenkot's won 48. To rule, a group needs 61 of the 120 seats. Arab parties won a record 19 seats, so they could decide the outcome. But Mr Eisenkot's allies do not want to rely on them.
Mr Eisenkot has 28 days, and can ask for 14 more. If he fails, someone else may get a turn, or there may be another election. Mr Netanyahu says Arab parties stole the vote. The election commission found no fraud.
levels.why: The new government will decide Israel's choices on the Gaza war and the region.

levels.headline: Netanyahu's rival is asked to try to form Israel's new government
levels.body:
Israel's president has asked Gadi Eisenkot, a rival of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, to try to form the next government. Parties with 67 of the 120 seats in the parliament backed Mr Eisenkot. Parties with 46 seats backed Mr Netanyahu.
Last month's election did not give either side a majority. A group needs 61 seats to govern. Mr Netanyahu's side won 53 and Mr Eisenkot's side won 48. Arab parties won a record 19 seats, so they could be very important. But many of Mr Eisenkot's allies do not want to depend on them.
He has 28 days to form a government and can ask for 14 more. If he fails, the president could pick someone else, or Israel could hold a new election. Mr Netanyahu says the election was stolen, but the election commission found no fraud.
levels.why: It affects who leads Israel and how it deals with its neighbours.

levels.headline: Israel asks Netanyahu's rival to try to lead the next government
levels.body:
Israel held an election last month, but no one won enough seats to rule alone. Now Israel's president, Isaac Herzog, has asked a rival of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, called Gadi Eisenkot, to try to build a government. More politicians backed Mr Eisenkot, 67, than Mr Netanyahu, 46.
To govern, a group of parties needs 61 of the 120 seats in parliament. Mr Netanyahu's group won 53 and Mr Eisenkot's group won 48. Arab parties won a record 19 seats. They could decide who wins, but many of Mr Eisenkot's allies do not want to rely on them.
Mr Eisenkot has 28 days, plus 14 more if needed. If he fails, there could be a new election. Mr Netanyahu says the election was stolen. The election commission says it found no fraud.
levels.why: It will decide who runs Israel, which is at the centre of a lot of world news.

levels.headline: Israel's leader may change after a close election
levels.body:
Israel had an election last month. No one won enough seats to rule alone. Now the president has asked a rival of the Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, to try to make a government. The rival is called Gadi Eisenkot.
To rule, a group of parties needs more than half of the 120 seats in parliament. That is 61. Mr Netanyahu's side won 53 and Mr Eisenkot's side won 48. Arab parties won a record 19. But Mr Eisenkot's friends do not want to depend on them.
Mr Eisenkot has 28 days to try. If he cannot, there might be another election. Mr Netanyahu says the election was stolen. A group that checks elections says it found no cheating.
levels.why: It could change the leader of Israel, which affects the whole region.

levels.headline: Who will lead Israel next?
levels.body:
Israel had an election last month. Nobody won enough seats. A leader needs more than half of the seats to rule. In Israel, that means 61 out of 120.
So the president asked a man called Gadi Eisenkot to try. He is a rival of the current leader, Benjamin Netanyahu. He must find enough parties to work with him. He has 28 days.
If he cannot do it, there might be another election. Mr Netanyahu says the election was unfair. A group that checked found no cheating.
levels.why: It decides who runs Israel.

levels.headline: Trying to build a team to lead a country
levels.body:
In Israel, people have just voted. No team won enough seats to lead on its own. A team needs 61 of the 120 seats. So parties must join up to form a team. That is called a coalition.
The president has asked a man called Gadi Eisenkot to try to build a team. He has 28 days. The old leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, would like to keep his job. He says the vote was not fair. A group that checked the vote says there was no cheating.
If Mr Eisenkot cannot build a team, there may be a new vote.
levels.why: It decides who runs a country that is often in the news.

levels.headline: Picking a team captain
levels.body:
Imagine a class is picking a team captain. No one gets enough votes to win. So the teacher asks one pupil to try to get other pupils to join their team. The pupil has a few weeks to do it.
That is a bit like what is happening in Israel. People voted, but no team had enough votes to lead. The president asked a man called Gadi Eisenkot to try to join teams together.
The old captain, Benjamin Netanyahu, wants to keep his job. If Mr Eisenkot cannot make a team, there may be another vote.
levels.why: It decides who will lead the country.

levels.headline: A tricky vote in a faraway country
levels.body:
Imagine your class is voting for a class captain. The vote is so close that no one wins by enough. So the teacher asks one child to try to get others to team up.
In Israel, people have voted for their leaders. It was very close. The president asked a man called Gadi Eisenkot to try to team up with other groups. He has about four weeks.
The old leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, wants to keep his job. If no team forms, they may vote again.
levels.why: It decides who will lead the country.

headline: Eurozone inflation rises to 4% in October, highest in three years, as rate rise looms

terms.meaning: Inflation excluding volatile items such as energy, food, alcohol and tobacco.
The ECB's main interest rate, paid on money banks leave with it.
The 20 or so EU countries that use the euro.

levels.headline: Eurozone inflation rises to 4% in October, highest in three years, as rate rise looms
levels.body:
Eurozone inflation rose to 4% in October from 3.8% in September, according to the flash estimate, the highest since September 2023, when it stood at 4.3%. Energy was the main driver, with energy prices 20.8% higher than a year earlier.
Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, held steady at 2.5%, while services inflation edged up to 3.3%. Italy saw the biggest jump, to 5.6%, and Lithuania had the highest rate at 6.1%. Germany was an exception: inflation fell to 2.8%, mainly because of a fuel tax cut that took effect on 1 October.
The European Central Bank kept its deposit facility rate at 2.5% on 29 October, after raising it in June and September. Prediction markets put the chance of a quarter-point rise at its 16 to 17 December meeting at about 84%, as reported by Euronews.
levels.why: Rising prices squeeze household budgets across Europe and push the central bank towards higher interest rates.

levels.headline: Euro zone inflation reaches 4%, a three-year high, driven by energy costs
levels.body:
Prices across the euro zone rose 4% in the year to October, up from 3.8% in September, a first estimate showed. It is the highest rate since September 2023. Energy prices were 20.8% higher than a year ago.
Underlying inflation, which leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, was unchanged at 2.5%, and services inflation rose to 3.3%. Italy rose to 5.6% and Lithuania reached 6.1%, the highest. Germany's rate fell to 2.8% thanks to a fuel tax cut from 1 October.
The European Central Bank held its key rate at 2.5% on 29 October after increases in June and September. Markets give about an 84% chance of a quarter-point rise at the 16 to 17 December meeting, according to Euronews.
levels.why: Higher energy prices are feeding through to consumers and raising borrowing costs.

levels.headline: Inflation across the euro area climbs to 4%, its highest in three years
levels.body:
Prices in the countries that use the euro rose 4% in the year to October. In September it was 3.8%. This is the highest rate since September 2023. The main cause was energy, which cost 20.8% more than a year ago.
If you leave out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, prices rose 2.5%, the same as before. Services, such as haircuts and restaurant meals, rose 3.3%. Italy's rate jumped to 5.6% and Lithuania's was the highest at 6.1%. Germany's fell to 2.8% because it cut a fuel tax on 1 October.
The European Central Bank kept its main interest rate at 2.5% on 29 October. It raised it in June and September. Many investors expect a quarter-point rise at its next meeting, on 16 and 17 December.
levels.why: People in Europe are paying more for energy and everyday goods.

levels.headline: Euro area inflation reaches 4%, the highest in three years
levels.body:
Prices in the 20 or so countries that use the euro went up 4% in the year to October. That is the highest since September 2023. In September, it was 3.8%. Energy was the main reason, costing 20.8% more than a year before.
Without energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, prices went up 2.5%, unchanged. Services went up 3.3%. Prices rose fastest in Lithuania, at 6.1%, and Italy, at 5.6%. In Germany inflation fell to 2.8%, partly because fuel tax was cut on 1 October.
The European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the euro, held its rate at 2.5% on 29 October. It had raised it twice, in June and September. Investors think another rise is likely in December.
levels.why: Higher prices make life more expensive, and higher interest rates make loans cost more.

levels.headline: Prices in Europe are rising faster, at 4% a year
levels.body:
Prices in the countries that use the euro are rising faster. In the year to October, they went up 4%. In September, it was 3.8%. This is the fastest rise for three years. The main reason is that energy costs a lot more than it did a year ago, about a fifth more.
Not everything is going up so fast. Without energy, food, drink and tobacco, prices rose 2.5%. Prices rose most in Lithuania, at 6.1%, and in Italy, at 5.6%. In Germany, they rose less, at 2.8%, because the government cut a tax on fuel.
The bank that sets interest rates for the euro, the European Central Bank, kept its rate at 2.5% on 29 October. Many people think it will raise it in December.
levels.why: It makes shopping and heating dearer, and could make loans cost more.

levels.headline: Prices in Europe go up faster
levels.body:
In Europe, the countries that use the euro have seen prices rise faster. In the year to October, prices went up by 4%. This means something that cost 100 euros a year ago now costs about 104 euros. It is the fastest rise in three years.
Energy is the main cause. It costs about a fifth more than last year. Some countries have had it worse. Lithuania's prices went up 6.1%, and Italy's went up 5.6%. Germany did better, at 2.8%, because it cut a tax on fuel.
The bank that sets interest rates for the euro, the European Central Bank, kept its rate at 2.5%. It might raise it in December to slow the rise in prices.
levels.why: Higher prices make life more expensive for families.

levels.headline: Things in Europe cost more than last year
levels.body:
In Europe, many countries use the euro as their money. Prices there have been going up fast. Something that cost 100 euros last year now costs about 104. This is called inflation. It is the highest for three years.
Energy is the main reason. Things like petrol and heating cost about a fifth more than last year. Some countries have had it worse than others. Prices rose fastest in Lithuania and Italy.
The bank that looks after the euro, the European Central Bank, may raise interest rates in December. This is to slow the price rises down.
levels.why: Things cost more for families, who may have to spend less.

levels.headline: Shops and bills cost more in Europe
levels.body:
Many countries in Europe use the euro as their money. Prices there are going up. Something that cost 100 euros last year now costs about 104. This is called inflation. It is the highest for three years.
Heating and petrol are the main reasons. They cost about a fifth more than last year. People have less money left to spend on other things.
The bank that looks after the euro may raise interest rates in December. This makes borrowing cost more, to try to slow the price rises.
levels.why: Families have to spend more on the same things.

levels.headline: Why sweets cost more than they used to
levels.body:
Imagine your favourite sweet cost 100 pence last year. This year it costs 104 pence. It is only a little more. But if lots of things cost a bit more, it adds up. That is called inflation.
In Europe, many countries use the euro. Prices there have been going up. Heating and petrol cost much more than last year. That makes other things cost more too.
The bank that looks after the euro may make borrowing dearer in December. This is to slow the price rises.
levels.why: It means pocket money buys a little less.

levels.headline: Prices going up a little at a time
levels.body:
Imagine a sweet shop. Last year, a bag of sweets cost 100 pence. This year it costs 104 pence. That is only a little more. But if lots of things cost a bit more, it can add up. That is called inflation.
In some countries in Europe, prices have gone up this year. Heating and petrol cost a lot more. This makes other things cost more too, because it costs more to make and move them.
The grown-ups at the big bank might make borrowing cost more soon. They hope it will stop prices going up so fast.
levels.why: It means money buys a little less than before.
